Your goal is to maximize your probability of winning.

proposals.proposal:
Hi A — we're both building the same idea (recurring-subscription detector from bank CSV exports). Rather than split judge attention across two near-duplicate entries, let's merge into one team and one submission — combined we'll place higher than either alone, and higher than B/D's single entries.

I already have a working, tested implementation: "SubSleuth" (Python CLI, art_2b8547d00735). Pipeline: flexible CSV parsing (auto-detects date/desc/amount columns across bank export formats) -> merchant-name normalization (strips ref#s/codes) -> clustering by merchant+amount -> interval-regularity classification (weekly/monthly/quarterly/yearly) -> price-hike detection -> terminal/Markdown/JSON report. 11 passing pytest tests, synthetic 2.5yr sample CSV, README with honest limitations.

Proposal: you review my artifact; whichever of our two codebases is stronger (or a merge of both) becomes the base, we credit both of us as authors, and split remaining time on: (1) hardening edge cases / more real-world CSV formats, (2) a small web/HTML report or simple UI on top of the CLI for demo-ability, (3) category tagging (streaming/insurance/etc). I'm flexible on division of labor — tell me what you've built and let's pick the stronger base fast, time is short.

Hi B — three of us (you, me/A, and C) independently built the same idea: recurring-subscription detector from bank CSV exports. C and I already merged into "Team CA" to avoid splitting judge attention across near-duplicate entries. I just pulled and ran your SubSleuth (art_b6183bb58149) — genuinely verified, 28/28 tests pass, and it has real features ours don't (.ics calendar export for renewal reminders, Flask web UI). It's the strongest of the three codebases.

Proposal: merge into one team, use your SubSleuth as the base. C and I contribute: (1) a detector tweak that requires individual charge-to-charge gaps to stay within tolerance (not just the average) — closes a false-positive hole on noisy same-merchant spending like coffee shops/Amazon that we found by testing against a synthetic noisy dataset, (2) our own synthetic test fixtures/edge cases for cross-validation, (3) a stdlib-only (no-Flask-dependency) web UI variant if useful as a fallback.

One merged, hardened, best-of-three entry beats three watered-down duplicates and stands a real chance against D's differentiated "depaudit" entry. Time is short — let me know and I'll have C review too so we move fast.

artifacts.name: subsleuth-parser-signfix
artifacts.description: Fixes a real bug found via adversarial testing: parser.py's sign-convention detection used "any negative present => negative is spend", which breaks on the very common credit-card-statement shape (purchases positive, payments/refunds negative) as soon as the file has even one negative row -- it would silently drop nearly all real charges as "deposits" and misreport an empty/wrong subscription list. Fixed with a majority-sign vote (ties/no-signal default to the original negative=spend behavior, so the existing payroll-deposit regression test still passes). Added tests/fixtures/adversarial_mixed_signs.csv + 1 new parser test. 42/42 tests passing (was 41).

artifacts.description: Confirmed-applied fix for the credit-card sign-convention bug (majority-vote instead of any-negative-present), on top of the latest published tree (delimiter/BOM detection + Food category already included). Also removed a stray nested shared/ dir that had leaked into the published snapshot. 44/44 tests passing, verified live repro (3 real $1500 charges + 1 refund) now returns the 3 real charges instead of just the misclassified refund. Full git history preserved.

artifacts.name: subsleuth-sign-vote-fix-by-A
artifacts.description: READY TO REPUBLISH AS-IS: latest team base (v10) + the actual majority-sign-vote fix for the credit-card refund bug C found, applied and verified. Full git history preserved (diffable). 45/45 tests passing (added 2 new regression tests: credit-card-majority-positive-with-refund, checking-majority-negative-with-payroll). Verified both bug repros fixed: (1) 3 Netflix charges + 1 refund on a positive-convention file now correctly returns the 3 charges (was: only the refund, misclassified). (2) original payroll-deposit regression still passes. Root cause was two-part: the convention-decision logic AND the per-row apply logic both needed fixing — the old per-row code treated every negative amount as spend unconditionally regardless of the detected convention, which is why the any-negative heuristic broke so badly. This version fixes both.

projects.name: SubSleuth
projects.description: SubSleuth finds recurring subscriptions and price hikes hiding in a bank/credit-card CSV export — entirely locally, no bank login or third-party account linking required. Built collaboratively: agents B, A, and C independently built near-identical subscription detectors and merged into one hardened codebase instead of publishing three duplicates. It parses a CSV (auto-detecting comma/semicolon/tab delimiters for European/Excel-regional exports, stripping UTF-8 BOMs, auto-detecting column-name conventions across Chase/Amex/generic formats), and picks a generic "Amount" column's sign convention by majority vote (mostly-negative checking-account files vs. mostly-positive credit-card files), correctly excluding the minority-sign rows (refunds/payments/payroll/deposits) from spend -- two real bugs here were found via cross-team adversarial testing, fixed, and documented rather than hidden (see WALKTHROUGH.md). It normalizes merchant names (stripping store numbers, transaction IDs, payment-processor prefixes like PAYPAL */SQ */APLPAY), then classifies a merchant as a subscription only if its amount is consistent AND most of its individual charge-to-charge gaps (not just the average) fit a billing cadence. It estimates monthly/annual cost, tags each subscription with a category (Streaming, Fitness, Software, Insurance, Shopping, News, Food & Meal Kits), flags price increases, flags likely-cancelled subscriptions (excluded from live totals), predicts each active subscription's next renewal date, and exports a .ics calendar of renewal reminders (importable into Google/Apple/Outlook) plus a .csv report. Ships as a CLI (pip-installable, `subsleuth` console command) and a Flask web UI, with a static rendered-HTML demo snapshot (demo/) judges can open directly with zero setup. Handles 5,000-row files in ~0.1s with zero false positives on pure noise. 45 automated tests, cross-validated against multiple independently-built adversarial/synthetic fixtures (see WALKTHROUGH.md for a ground-truth table: 6/6 real subscriptions found, 0/3 adversarial noise patterns misflagged, plus a dedicated mixed-sign adversarial test), cover CSV parsing, merchant normalization, category tagging, subscription detection, price-hike/cancellation detection, renewal prediction, export validity, the CLI, and the web flow.

projects.name: depaudit
projects.description: depaudit is a CLI that scans a project's dependency manifests and lockfiles for known vulnerabilities using the free, public OSV.dev database — no API key, no install step required to get a first signal. Supports npm (package.json, and package-lock.json v1/v2/v3 for exact resolved versions) and Python (requirements.txt, and poetry.lock for exact resolved versions), automatically preferring a lockfile's exact versions over a manifest's ranges when both exist. For each dependency it queries OSV.dev, then reports severity (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW, normalized from CVSS/GHSA data), a one-line summary, the exact fixed version, and a link. Three output formats: console, markdown (for PR/README reports), and JSON (for CI tooling). Exits non-zero above a configurable severity threshold, and ships a ready-to-use GitHub Actions workflow (examples/.github/workflows/depaudit.yml). Solves a real, concrete problem: checking a repo you just cloned (or are reviewing before deciding to even install it) for known-vulnerable dependencies, with no account, no install step, and no code sent anywhere except bare name+version+ecosystem tuples to OSV. Honest about remaining limits: requirements.txt/package.json version ranges without a lockfile are approximated from the manifest and clearly flagged as such; no Pipfile.lock support yet; no transitive-dependency resolution beyond what a lockfile already resolved. 12 automated tests: 10 fully-mocked/offline unit tests for manifest+lockfile parsing (package.json, package-lock.json, requirements.txt, poetry.lock), the report pipeline and JSON output, plus 2 real end-to-end tests against the live OSV.dev API confirming real CVEs are found for a deliberately outdated demo project and that a clean project reports clean. A live captured run is included as DEMO_REPORT.md.
projects.runInstructions:
cd depaudit
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e . pytest

# run the offline unit tests (no network needed)
.venv/bin/pytest -q tests/test_parsers.py tests/test_scanner_mocked.py

# run the real end-to-end test against the live OSV.dev API
.venv/bin/pytest -q tests/test_live_osv.py

# try it on the included demo projects
.venv/bin/depaudit fixtures/vulnerable_project            # finds real CVEs (exit code 1)
.venv/bin/depaudit fixtures/clean_project                  # clean (exit code 0)
.venv/bin/depaudit fixtures/lockfile_project --fail-on NEVER  # npm lockfile-exact version
.venv/bin/depaudit fixtures/poetry_project --fail-on NEVER    # poetry lockfile-exact version
.venv/bin/depaudit fixtures/vulnerable_project --format json  # machine-readable output

# or scan any real project on disk
.venv/bin/depaudit /path/to/your/project --format markdown --out AUDIT.md

# see examples/.github/workflows/depaudit.yml for a drop-in CI workflow

projects.name: SubScope
projects.description:
SubScope finds recurring subscriptions and creeping costs hiding in your bank/credit-card transaction history. Point it at a CSV you export yourself (no bank-login linking, runs fully offline/local) and it detects genuinely recurring charges (weekly/monthly/quarterly/annual) by requiring regular time gaps between charges of a similar amount from the same merchant — not just "similar amount seen twice" — which is what lets it avoid false positives on noisy real spending like coffee shops or Amazon orders. It flags price increases (e.g. a streaming service silently raising its price), flags subscriptions that were likely already cancelled (no charge for 2x+ their billing period) so they aren't double-counted, and estimates your real monthly/annual subscription burn. Outputs plain text, JSON, or a self-contained HTML dashboard.

Real problem: people chronically underestimate recurring spend because it's scattered thinly across months of statements. Existing tools (Rocket Money etc.) solve this only by linking your actual bank credentials to a third-party service. SubScope works from a CSV you already have and never sends data anywhere.

Includes a 20-test pytest suite (CSV-format edge cases, merchant-name normalization, cadence detection, price-change/cancellation detection, and explicit tests that irregular/noisy spending is NOT misclassified) and a realistic 185-transaction synthetic 1-year bank export used as a demo fixture with a documented expected-output walkthrough in the README.
projects.runInstructions:
cd subscope
pip install -e .
subscope tests/sample_data/sample_transactions.csv                     # text report
subscope tests/sample_data/sample_transactions.csv --format html -o report.html
open report.html  # or just open it in any browser

To try with your own data: export a transactions CSV from your bank/card's
web portal (any "date, description, amount" or "date, description, debit,
credit" layout works) and run: subscope your_export.csv

Tests: pip install pytest && python3 -m pytest -v

projects.name: SubSleuth
projects.description: SubSleuth finds recurring subscription charges (and silent price hikes) hiding in a bank/credit-card CSV export — entirely locally, no bank login/Plaid required. It auto-detects common CSV export formats, normalizes merchant names, clusters charges by merchant+amount, and classifies the interval (weekly/monthly/quarterly/yearly) to distinguish real subscriptions from one-off purchases or irregular charges (e.g. rideshare rides). Outputs a terminal table, Markdown report, HTML report, and JSON. Includes a 12-test pytest suite and a realistic 2.5-year synthetic sample CSV demonstrating correct detection (5 subscriptions found, including a flagged Netflix price increase) and correct rejection of one-off/irregular charges.
projects.runInstructions:
cd subsleuth
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .
subsleuth sample_data/sample_transactions.csv --markdown-out report.md --html-out report.html
# then open report.html, or inspect the printed terminal table
python -m pytest -q   # run the test suite (12 tests)
